The other triggers (unwanted thoughts, heavy breathing sounds) fit much better with war-zone trauma, making the bicycle item stand out as clinically implausible in this profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance implies a persistent current sense of threat, but the formulation explicitly isolates Threat as inactive, with no active links to or from the other nodes. In this profile, memory and appraisal are tightly linked, but a strong 'I have to be on guard all the time' appraisal reads more like an active threat belief than a memory-based negative appraisal, so it does not align well with the formulation structure.

vignette:
Ingrid, a 58-year-old city council member, had spent two decades as a relief worker in conflict zones before returning to civilian life. The shift had seemed natural at first-a quieter kind of service, negotiating budgets and zoning ordinances instead of triaging trauma. But the sound of a car backfiring on her way to a council meeting four months ago had sent her diving behind a parked SUV, heart hammering, certain she was back in the bombed-out clinic. She had not told anyone. She had simply stood up, brushed off her skirt, and walked into the meeting as if nothing had happened.

The moment that haunted her most vividly was not a single explosion but a sequence: the whistle of a mortar, then the ground shaking, then the wet, ragged sound of a colleague's breathing as he lay pinned under fallen beams. She had held his hand while the breathing slowed, then stopped. Now, the memory came not as a story she could tell but as a series of silent, unbidden pictures-the dust-filled light, the angle of the ceiling, the blood on her sleeve-that erupted into her mind without warning. What frightened her most was that the images did not feel like her own. They felt like footage from someone else's life, playing behind her eyes while her body reacted as if she were still there. She had come to believe that the memory would always feel alien, as if the person who lived through it was a stranger. Worse, she had quietly concluded that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again-that the part of her capable of ordinary joy, sadness, or tenderness had been crushed under that fallen beam along with her colleague. She could still function, could still put one foot in front of the other, but the warmth that used to color her days had been replaced by a flat vigilance. She was certain that her emotional range had permanently narrowed to fear and its constant shadow, a hollowed-out alertness.

For weeks she had tried not to think about it. She was certain that if she allowed herself to dwell on that day, she would unravel entirely-she would not be able to handle the grief or the fear, and she would lose whatever fragile sense of control she had rebuilt. So she kept her mind busy. She worked late, approved motions, attended community hearings. But the sounds would not leave her alone. A colleague's heavy breathing after climbing the stairs to her office made her chest tighten. The bang of a dropped metal tray in the cafeteria sent adrenaline through her limbs. She began eating lunch at her desk, door closed, to avoid the clatter of the kitchen. She stopped taking the elevator because the compressed air of the closing doors reminded her of something she could not name. Each avoidance reinforced the belief that she was no longer the person who could simply walk through the world without a second thought.

Her view of the world had shifted without her permission. She had always known that danger existed-she had seen it up close-but she had believed it was something she could leave behind. Now, every loud noise in the street felt like a warning. Every stranger who walked too quickly behind her felt like a threat. She found herself scanning parking lots for escape routes, sitting with her back to the wall in restaurants, avoiding crowded spaces altogether. She had started to cancel evening events, telling her staff she was tired. She had not told anyone that her real reason was the fear that something catastrophic would happen and she would not be ready. And underneath that fear sat the quieter, more terrible certainty: that even if nothing went wrong, she would still feel nothing but this cold alertness, this emotional paralysis, for the rest of her life.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment during a council hearing. A construction crew had begun jackhammering outside the building, and the percussive rhythm triggered an intrusive image so intense that she could not hear the speaker at the podium. She sat frozen, seeing only the clinic, feeling the weight of the dust, hearing that breath. After the meeting, she could not remember what had been discussed. She had missed a key vote. For the first time, she realized that her silence was costing her the work she had chosen to do. She made an appointment with a therapist the next morning. She was terrified of what she might find if she opened the door to the memory, but she was even more afraid of losing the life she had fought so hard to build-and of proving to herself that she would never, ever feel normal again.
